ADS 6703 · Natural Language Processing · Workshop 6

Which words mean the same?

Word vectors and word2vec

Thursday 19 November 2026 · Sessions 19–21

Agenda

  • Fill in the blank
  • A word's neighbours: word vectors by counting
  • Word2vec's guessing game
  • What word vectors learn: products, analogies, limits
  • Lab

Fill in the blank

"I'll have a ___ latte, please."

Let the class shout answers. Expect iced, hot, cold, large, decaf. Then ask: how did you know which words fit? Nobody gave you a dictionary definition; you have seen these words used around "latte" many times.

The words that fit

"I'll have a ___ latte, please.": iced, cold, hot, large, decaf

You never looked up what iced means. You have seen it, many times, next to latte, tea and coffee.

Words that fit the same blanks are used in the same way.

A word is known by its neighbours

"You shall know a word by the company it keeps."

J. R. Firth, linguist, 1957

So describe each word by the words that appear around it.

This idea is called the distributional hypothesis. The name is not needed for the exam; the idea is.

What a spelling match sees

A customer searches for cold tea.

Menu item Words shared with cold tea
iced tea with lemon tea
cold coffee with milk cold

Both share one word. Nothing says that cold and iced mean nearly the same.

With TF-IDF, "cold" is often the rarer word, so cold coffee can even win. Word vectors fix this by giving cold and iced similar numbers.

A word's neighbours

Describe a word by counting the words next to it.

Six café orders

Order
1 iced latte please
2 cold latte please
3 iced tea please
4 cold tea please
5 cold water please
6 lemon cake please

A word's neighbours: the word just before it and the word just after it.

iced and cold are never in the same order.

Count each word's neighbours

iced latte please · cold latte please · iced tea please · cold tea please · cold water please · lemon cake please

latte tea water cake
iced 1 1 0 0
cold 1 1 1 0
lemon 0 0 0 1

Each row is a list of numbers: the word's vector.

Columns that are 0 for all three words (iced, cold, lemon, please) are left out to fit the slide. The full vector has one number for every word of the vocabulary.

Exercise: neighbours of latte and tea

iced latte please · cold latte please · iced tea please · cold tea please · cold water please · lemon cake please

Count the neighbours of latte and of tea, under the words iced, cold and please.

iced cold please
latte 1 1 2
tea 1 1 2

The same numbers: latte and tea are used in exactly the same way here.

iced against cold: dot product

latte tea water cake
iced 1 1 0 0
cold 1 1 1 0

1×1 + 1×1 + 0×1 + 0×0 = 2

Multiply number by number, then add up.

iced against cold: lengths and cosine

Lengths: √(1 + 1) ≈ 1.41 and √(1 + 1 + 1) ≈ 1.73

\[ \cos = \frac{a \cdot b}{|a| \times |b|} = \frac{2}{1.41 \times 1.73} = \frac{2}{2.45} \approx \mathbf{0.82} \]

Two words that never appear together, and yet a cosine of 0.82.

iced against lemon

latte tea water cake
iced 1 1 0 0
lemon 0 0 0 1

Dot product: 0 + 0 + 0 + 0 = 0, so the cosine is 0

No neighbours in common: nothing alike.

The catch: very long vectors

  • One number for every word of the vocabulary
  • A real vocabulary has 50,000 words or more: 50,000 numbers per word, almost all 0
  • A word seen only a few times gets a vector of almost nothing but 0s

These count vectors are called sparse: mostly zeros. Word2vec gives dense vectors: few numbers, none of them zero.

Word2vec

Learn a short list of numbers for every word, by playing a guessing game.

Word2vec was published by Mikolov and colleagues at Google in 2013. The version taught here is skip-gram with negative sampling, SLP section 5.5.

The guessing game

"Is this a real neighbour pair, or a fake one?"

Pair Where it comes from Answer
(iced, latte) the text: iced latte please real
(iced, cake) iced with a random word fake

The game itself is not the point. What we keep are the numbers the model learns while playing it.

Real pairs come straight from the text, so no one has to label anything. Fake pairs are made up by picking a random word.

Each word gets a short list

Start with small numbers. Two numbers per word, to keep it simple:

Word List
iced [1, 0]
latte [0, 1]

The score of a pair is the dot product: 1×0 + 0×1 = 0

Real pairs should get big scores, fake pairs small ones.

Real word2vec uses 100 to 300 numbers per word and starts them at small random values. Our lab uses 5.

The sigmoid: from a score to a chance

\[ \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} \]

score x −2 −1 −0.5 0 0.5 1 2
σ(x) 0.12 0.27 0.38 0.50 0.62 0.73 0.88

Any score becomes a number between 0 and 1: the model's guess that the pair is real.

e is about 2.718. The values are given in the exam. A score of 0 gives 0.5: no idea either way.

Exercise: read the guess

The score of (iced, latte) is 2. The score of (iced, cake) is −1. What does the model guess for each?

(iced, latte): σ(2) = 0.88, fairly sure it is real

(iced, cake): σ(−1) = 0.27, fairly sure it is fake

The nudge

After each guess, move both lists a little, so the next guess is better.

  • target: 1 for a real pair, 0 for a fake pair; error = target − guess
  • Each list moves by rate × error × the other list

\[ w_{\text{new}} = w + \text{rate} \times \text{error} \times c \qquad c_{\text{new}} = c + \text{rate} \times \text{error} \times w \]

w is the word's list, c is the neighbour's list. Both updates use the old numbers. The rate keeps each step small; 0.5 here so the numbers are easy, about 0.05 in the lab. This is gradient descent on the logistic loss, but students don't need that name.

One nudge, by hand: the guess

Real pair (iced, latte). iced = [1, 0], latte = [0, 1], rate = 0.5.

  • Score: 1×0 + 0×1 = 0
  • Guess: σ(0) = 0.50
  • Error: target − guess = 1 − 0.50 = 0.50

One nudge, by hand: the new lists

rate × error = 0.5 × 0.50 = 0.25

iced: [1, 0] + 0.25 × [0, 1] = [1, 0] + [0, 0.25] = [1, 0.25]

latte: [0, 1] + 0.25 × [1, 0] = [0, 1] + [0.25, 0] = [0.25, 1]

latte moves using iced's OLD list [1, 0], not the new one.

One nudge, by hand: the new guess

iced = [1, 0.25], latte = [0.25, 1]

Score: 1×0.25 + 0.25×1 = 0.25 + 0.25 = 0.5

Guess: σ(0.5) = 0.62, up from 0.50

A real pair: the two lists moved towards each other, and the guess got better.

The picture: the two arrows turn towards each other

The angle between them closes from 90° to about 62°.

Dashed: before. Solid: after one nudge. cos = 0.5 ÷ (1.03 × 1.03) ≈ 0.47, which is about 62°.

Exercise: a fake pair

Fake pair (iced, cake). iced = [1, 0], cake = [0, 1], rate = 0.5. The target is now 0.

Score 0, guess σ(0) = 0.50, error = 0 − 0.50 = −0.50, rate × error = −0.25

iced: [1, 0] − 0.25 × [0, 1] = [1, −0.25]   cake: [0, 1] − 0.25 × [1, 0] = [−0.25, 1]

New score: −0.25 − 0.25 = −0.5, new guess σ(−0.5) = 0.38, down from 0.50

Same start as the real pair, so the numbers are easy to compare. A fake pair pushes the two arrows apart: the angle opens past 90°.

Why iced ends up close to cold

  • iced is nudged towards latte, tea and coffee, again and again
  • cold is nudged towards the same words
  • So the two lists end up pointing the same way, though iced and cold never meet

Fake pairs push every word away from random words, so words with different neighbours drift apart.

Two lists per word

Every word has two lists of numbers:

  • one for when it is the word: iced in (iced, latte)
  • one for when it is the neighbour: latte in (iced, latte)
  • At the end, the first list is kept: that is the word vector

With a single list, a word's score with itself would always be high, and words would be pushed to be their own neighbours. SLP calls the two matrices W and C. Some systems add W and C at the end instead.

Real word2vec

By hand 30,000 reviews Large models
Text 6 orders 1.2 million words billions of words
Numbers per word 2 100 100 to 300
Fake pairs per real pair 1 5 5 to 20
Neighbours 1 each side 5 each side 5 to 10 each side

The same nudge each time, only repeated many more times.

Pretrained vectors (Google News word2vec, GloVe, fastText) are free to download, so a company rarely trains its own from scratch.

Trained on 30,000 appliance reviews

Word Closest words (cosine)
fridge refrigerator 0.95, frig 0.86, refrig 0.78, refridgerator 0.77
keurig kuerig 0.84, kurig 0.79, keruig 0.78
gift birthday 0.79, christmas 0.79
easy simple 0.75, quick 0.70, painless 0.69

No one told the model any of this. It only saw which words sit next to which.

gensim, skip-gram, 100 numbers, window 5, 5 fake pairs, 5 passes, about 10 seconds on a laptop. Keurig is a coffee-machine brand; the model learned the misspellings customers type. A search for "easy fridge" can now find "the frig was a simple setup".

Back to cold and iced

In the 30,000 reviews:

cosine(cold, iced) = 0.62

The two words a spelling match can't connect now have similar vectors, learned from the text alone.

Closest to cold in the reviews: warm 0.76, hot 0.73. That is the next problem: opposites.

What word vectors learn

Products, analogies, and two things they get wrong.

A customer's products as a sentence

Customer A: AeroPress · metal filter · milk frother    Customer B: AeroPress · paper filters

Each customer's list of products is a sentence, each product a word, every other product in the list a neighbour.

Products bought by the same kinds of customers get vectors that point the same way.

This is item2vec (Barkan and Koenigstein, 2016). Airbnb learned listing vectors the same way, from the listings people click in one search session (Grbovic and Cheng, 2018). It needs no product descriptions, only what people buy or click.

"You may also like", from 8,128 real customers

Product Closest product vectors
AeroPress coffee maker reusable metal filters for the AeroPress 0.78
Nespresso refill-your-own-capsule kit its paper filters 0.96, foil seals 0.94, caps 0.93
GE MWF fridge water filter other filters that fit the same fridges 0.78

Learned only from who reviewed what. The model never read a product name.

The capsule kit, its filters, seals and caps are bought together by the same people. A text search on descriptions would not link a coffee maker with "The DISC" or "The MESH", the names of two of its filters. Customers who reviewed one product only are left out: they have no neighbours.

Analogies: arithmetic with meanings

With vectors learned from billions of words:

king − man + woman ≈ queen

Paris − France + Italy ≈ Rome

The difference between two vectors can stand for a relation: male → female, country → capital.

SLP section 5.7. It works for frequent words and common relations, and often fails for others; it is a nice illustration, not a reliable tool. ≈ means the closest vector, leaving out the three input words.

Opposites end up close

Pair Cosine in the 30,000 reviews
hot, cold 0.73
good, bad 0.59
happy, unhappy 0.76

Opposites are used in the same places (hot water, cold water; I was happy, I was unhappy), so their vectors come out close.

Word vectors know which words are used alike, not which ones mean the same. A search for cold tea may return hot tea.

happy's closest words are pleased 0.88, satisfied 0.83, then unhappy 0.76 and disappointed 0.71. A problem for sentiment: word vectors alone don't separate good from bad.

Vectors learn our biases

Vectors learned from news text gave:

man : computer programmer :: woman : homemaker

  • The vectors copy the patterns of the text they read, including unfair ones
  • A hiring tool that ranks CVs with them could score women lower for a programming job

Bolukbasi et al., 2016, on Google News word2vec vectors. SLP section 5.8. Manager's lens: ask what text a model learned from, and test it on cases where bias would hurt.

Recap

  • A word is described by its neighbours: count them, and the counts are its vector
  • Word2vec learns a short vector per word with a guessing game: real pairs against fake ones
  • guess = σ(dot product); error = target − guess; each list moves by rate × error × the other list
  • Words with the same neighbours get similar vectors: fridge and refrigerator, cold and iced

What word vectors get wrong

  • Opposites, like hot and cold, come out close: used alike, opposite in meaning
  • Each word gets one vector, whatever it means in the sentence
  • They copy the biases of the text they learn from

One vector per word: "bank" of a river and "bank" for money share a vector. Transformers (W8) give each word a vector that depends on the sentence around it.
